items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy has had 2 days of painful urination, urinary frequency and grossly bloody urine. A week ago he had fever, sore throat and red eyes, and two classmates had the same illness. He is afebrile now, and blood pressure is 102/64 mmHg. Urinalysis shows many red blood cells with normal shapes, a few white blood cells and no casts. Bacterial urine culture is negative, and serum creatinine is 0.4 mg/dL. Which of the following best describes the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.html: Enveloped virus with a segmented negative-sense RNA genome

options.label: B
options.html: Enveloped virus with a single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome

options.label: D
options.html: Nonenveloped virus with a double-stranded linear DNA genome

options.label: E
options.html: Nonenveloped virus with a single-stranded DNA genome

items.explanationHtml:
Hemorrhagic cystitis after pharyngoconjunctival fever in a child is typical of adenovirus, a nonenveloped virus with linear double-stranded DNA. Normally shaped red cells, no casts, a normal creatinine and a sterile bacterial culture place the bleeding in the bladder rather than the glomerulus. The illness resolves on its own in about 1–2 weeks; in transplant recipients adenovirus and BK virus cause more severe hemorrhagic cystitis.

Takeaway: gross hematuria with dysuria and a negative bacterial culture after pharyngoconjunctivitis in a child is adenoviral hemorrhagic cystitis.

whyNot.A: Segmented negative-sense RNA viruses (influenza, bunyaviruses) do not cause hemorrhagic cystitis; hantaviruses affect the kidney through interstitial nephritis with fever and shock.
whyNot.B: Positive-sense RNA viruses such as enteroviruses cause conjunctivitis and pharyngitis but not hemorrhagic cystitis.
whyNot.C: E. coli cystitis would grow on routine bacterial culture.
whyNot.E: Parvovirus B19, the single-stranded DNA virus, causes erythema infectiosum and aplastic crisis, not cystitis.

items.objective: Recognise adenovirus as a cause of hemorrhagic cystitis in children and describe its structure.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with an indwelling urinary catheter is treated with intravenous ceftriaxone for fever and suprapubic pain. After 3 days he is still febrile. Urine and blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains that are catalase negative, grow in 6.5% sodium chloride and hydrolyse esculin in the presence of bile. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

options.label: A
options.html: Efflux pumps that remove fluoroquinolones from the cell

options.label: B
options.html: Low-affinity penicillin-binding proteins in the cell wall

options.label: C
options.html: Methylation of the 23S ribosomal RNA target

items.explanationHtml:
The organism is Enterococcus (catalase-negative cocci in chains that grow in high salt and bile esculin), a common cause of catheter-associated and post-instrumentation UTI. Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins because their penicillin-binding proteins (notably PBP5) bind cephalosporins poorly. Ampicillin is the usual drug for susceptible strains.

Takeaway: cephalosporins never cover enterococci, because their penicillin-binding proteins bind cephalosporins poorly.

whyNot.A: Efflux pumps cause fluoroquinolone and tetracycline resistance, not failure of ceftriaxone.
whyNot.C: Ribosomal methylation (erm genes) causes macrolide and clindamycin resistance.
whyNot.D: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases are made by gram-negative rods such as E. coli and Klebsiella, not by enterococci.
whyNot.E: The D-Ala-D-Lac change is the mechanism of vancomycin resistance (VRE), which is not the drug used here.

items.objective: Explain the intrinsic cephalosporin resistance of Enterococcus in urinary tract infection.
